description: Whether one party or every party must consent before a call is recorded, by US state, DC and Canadian province, plus the US federal rule and the interstate rule of thumb.
disclaimer: Informational, not legal advice. Laws change and courts interpret them; confirm with a lawyer licensed in the jurisdiction before relying on any rule here.
generated: Generated by the export script from the rule source. Do not edit by hand; propose changes as described in CONTRIBUTING.md.

federal.bottom_line: Federal law lets a party to a call record it, unless the recording is made to commit a crime or a tort. It is a floor: stricter state all-party laws still apply.
federal.quote: It shall not be unlawful under this chapter for a person not acting under color of law to intercept a wire, oral, or electronic communication where such person is a party to the communication

interstate.rule: When any party to the call is in an all-party state, follow that state's rule for the whole call. The practical standard is a spoken recording notice at the start of every recorded call, captured inside the recording, in every state.
interstate.authority: Kearney v. Salomon Smith Barney, Inc., 39 Cal.4th 95 (2006): California law applied to calls recorded in a one-party state with California clients, and a notice at the outset of the call complies.
interstate.quote: a business can comply with the applicable California statute by providing such information at the outset of a telephone conversation so that the client or customer will not have a reasonable expectation that the conversation is not being recorded
interstate.supporting: RCW 9.73.030(1)(a) reaches communications 'between points within or without the state', so Washington's statute covers interstate calls by its terms.

rules.bottom_line: A business that is a party to the call may record it without telling the other side. Callers in all-party states still bring their own state's rule with them.
rules.quote: To overhear, record, amplify or transmit any part of the private communication of others without the consent of at least one of the persons engaged in the communication
rules.detail: Eavesdropping is recording others without the consent of at least one participant.

rules.detail: 632 requires every party's consent to record a confidential communication. 632.7 requires every party's consent to record any call involving a cellular or cordless phone, confidential or not. leginfo.legislature.ca.gov refused automated reads; read on FindLaw (current to 2026-01-01).

rules.bottom_line: For phone calls, play a verbal notice that is captured at the start of the recording, as 52-570d(a)(2) allows.

rules.bottom_line: Both statutes are on the books, so treat Delaware as all-party and announce the recording at the start of the call.

Separately, the Privacy Commissioner says a business recording customer calls under PIPEDA "must inform the customer that they are recording a call, clearly state the purpose of the recording and obtain consent" (https://www.priv.gc.ca/en/privacy-topics/surveillance/02_05_d_14/, updated 2026-10-08). Provincial private-sector privacy laws in Quebec, Alberta and British Columbia were not checked.
